title: Analyze
text:
Evidence and interpretation
The draft workflow is informed by the existing resource catalog, including The Turing Way, Good Enough Practices in Scientific Computing, the TIER Protocol, FAIR Principles for Research Software, RDMkit, DataONE, and Ecological Forecasting Initiative guidance. These sources support clear objectives, recorded code and settings, reproducible execution, and traceable results. They inform this draft workflow but do not establish GeoEpi or institutional policy. Access date: 2026-08-06.

title: Analyze
text:
Ready-for-validation gate
The safe starting status is not ready for validation. Use only these statuses:

not ready for validation
ready for validation
ready for validation with documented limitation

An analysis may enter future Validate only when:

The question or practical objective is recorded.
The quantity, comparison, prediction, pattern, or simulation outcome is clear.
The dataset ID, version, readiness status, and limitation are recorded.
Exploratory, planned, sensitivity, and post hoc work are labeled appropriately.
Methods, variables, transformations, exclusions, settings, and intended outputs are recorded.
Consequential changes made after viewing results are documented.
Code, settings, software, and computing information can be identified.
Consequential executions have run IDs or a clearly repeatable execution path.
Seeds, scenarios, parameter sets, partitions, and replicates are recorded where applicable.
Expected and produced outputs are compared.
Warnings, failures, retries, cancellations, and incomplete runs are visible.
Important candidate results have traceability records where warranted, and their result IDs are named in the analysis-level readiness decision.
Limitations and unresolved execution problems are visible.
The analysis specification or equivalent analysis-level record is authoritative for readiness.
A responsible analyst or reviewer records the readiness decision and ISO 8601 decision time in that analysis-level record.
Status is explicitly recorded as one of the three statuses above.

Run completion belongs to the run record. Candidate selection belongs to result records and the analysis-level readiness decision. Passing this gate means that the analysis has been specified, executed, and recorded well enough to undergo validation. It does not mean that the analysis has passed validation.

title: Results and Traceability
text:
A result record connects an important reported value, figure, table, map, forecast, simulation summary, or operational product to the data, code, settings, execution, and output that produced it.
analysis-ready dataset
  -> analysis specification
  -> code and settings
  -> analysis run
  -> output
  -> candidate result

title: Results and Traceability
text:
A result record connects an important reported value, figure, table, map, forecast, simulation summary, or operational product to the data, code, settings, execution, and output that produced it.
analysis-ready dataset
  -> analysis specification
  -> code and settings
  -> analysis run
  -> output
  -> candidate result

title: Results and Traceability
text:
When to create one
A result record is useful when an output is included in a manuscript, shared outside the immediate team, used in an operational decision, used in a presentation or report, compared across scenarios, expensive to regenerate, likely to be revised, or consequential to the project’s conclusion. Not every temporary plot requires a separate record. Closely related outputs may share one record when their inputs, run, status, and interpretation are the same.

title: Results and Traceability
text:
Result identity
Record as appropriate: result ID and name, analysis ID and version, direct input dataset IDs and versions, code version, settings or parameter record, computing environment, run ID, output location, intended use, status, limitations, and a later result that supersedes it. Source lineage remains available through the staged- or derived-dataset record and does not need to be repeated in every result row. A filename alone is not a sufficient result identity. The result traceability template is a compact starting point.

title: Results and Traceability
text:
Result statuses
Use planned, produced, incomplete, candidate for validation, failed, or superseded. The safe default is planned. Produced means the output exists. Candidate for validation means the analysis-level readiness decision selected the result for checking in Validate. Validation itself has not yet occurred.
Keep the levels distinct: a run status describes what happened during one execution; a result status describes what happened to one output; analysis readiness describes whether the documented analysis and its named candidate results may enter Validate. The analysis specification or equivalent analysis-level record is the authoritative readiness decision. Candidate result IDs should be referenced by the validation plan and validation decisions and records.

title: Results and Traceability
text:
Manuscripts and reports
Copying a figure into a manuscript does not preserve its origin. Point the result record to the actual output file, keep captions and table notes consistent with the analysis version, document manually altered figures or tables, and link reported numbers to the same run and result version as the displayed output.

title: Results and Traceability
text:
Superseded results
Do not delete the only record of an earlier result when it influenced a decision, appeared in a draft, was shared externally, was replaced after a correction, or differs because data, code, settings, or scenarios changed. Mark it superseded and identify the replacement.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text: Distinguish source ID, snapshot ID, staged-dataset ID, dataset version, derived-dataset ID, transformation ID, run ID, and output ID. A filename alone is usually not a sufficient stable identifier.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text: Distinguish source ID, snapshot ID, staged-dataset ID, dataset version, derived-dataset ID, transformation ID, run ID, and output ID. A filename alone is usually not a sufficient stable identifier.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text:
Record identifiers
Document natural, surrogate, composite, repeated-observation, hierarchical, spatial-unit, temporal, sample, sequence, facility, herd, animal, case, and observation identifiers as applicable. Do not construct identifiers from sensitive fields unless authorized.
For each important key, state whether it is unique, unique within a group, repeatable across time, nonmissing, stable across snapshots, supplied by the source or generated locally, and safe to disclose.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text:
Duplicates and relationships
Distinguish byte-for-byte duplicate files, duplicate rows, legitimate repeated observations, duplicate identifiers, conflicting records, revised records, and multiple reports of one event. Identical values are not automatically duplicate observations.
Document primary keys, foreign keys, relationship cardinality, expected match rate, unmatched records, many-to-many joins, deduplication before joining, aggregation order, and snapshot/temporal compatibility.






Stop and resolve



An accidental many-to-many join can multiply records while producing plausible-looking outputs. Stop when join losses, unexpected multiplication, or conflicting keys cannot be explained.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text:
Schema definition
Build on the existing data dictionary template. A usable schema documents field name, description, type, unit, allowed values/codes, missing-value convention, identifier role, date/time convention, spatial meaning, temporal support, derivation, quality notes, and schema version where warranted.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text:
Types and parsing
Review automatic type guessing for consequential datasets. Check strings with leading zeroes, categorical codes, locale-dependent numbers, dates, Boolean values, censored values, scientific notation, large integers, coordinate precision, and encoding.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text:
Units and missingness
Record unit definition, scale, denominator where relevant, original and standardized units, conversion rule, and mixed-unit handling. Distinguish not observed, not applicable, suppressed, below detection, not reported, withheld, structurally absent, parsing failure, and true zero. Do not collapse these states without recording the consequence.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text:
Categorical codes and schema versions
For each code, record code, label, definition, source/version, valid period when codes change, and handling of unknown or deprecated values. Create a new schema version when fields, types, units, code meanings, identifier meanings, temporal support, or spatial support affect interpretation or compatibility.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text:
Domain examples

Surveillance records: case ID, case-definition version, facility/jurisdiction key, event/report dates, and revision status.
Field observations: observation ID, taxon ID, site key, effort, unit, and detection-limit convention.
Sequence metadata: sample ID, accession, host/location restriction, collection date, and reference version.
Spatial polygons: stable area ID, boundary version, CRS, geometry status, and spatial support.
Weekly rasters: tile/layer ID, week-year, CRS, origin/alignment, NoData, and mask.
Simulation inputs: scenario ID, parameter-set version, units, and initial/boundary conditions.

title: Project and Data Structure
text: Structure should allow a reviewer or future collaborator to determine which objects were received, transformed, authoritative, temporary, regenerable, or used to support a reported result.

title: Project and Data Structure
text:
Define object roles







Role
Meaning and minimum control




Preserved source
Original received representation, retained without undocumented editing, linked to source and snapshot IDs, and subject to access restrictions.


Staged
Controlled representation produced from the preserved source; suitable for normalization, linkage, and structural QA, but not necessarily analysis-ready.


Derived
Dataset created through documented transformation, such as aggregates, features, standardized layers, or linked data.


Analysis-ready
Staged or derived data that passed the Organize gate; this status is not scientific validation.


Configuration
Paths, parameters, conventions, source IDs, and transformation settings.


Documentation
README, data dictionary, dataset record, transformation ledger, decisions, limitations, and QA results.


Outputs
Consequential products produced by analysis or reporting; not interchangeable with staged or derived data.


Logs
Execution, warnings, failures, retries, checks, and manual interventions.


Cache or temporary
Removable or regenerable objects whose role is documented and which are not the only copy of a consequential object.

title: Project and Data Structure
text:
No universal folder tree
The Lab Book does not prescribe one universal directory tree. Every project must document the role of each major location, which location is authoritative, which objects are tracked in Git, which are stored externally, which are generated, which are temporary, and how protected data are separated.

title: Project and Data Structure
text:
Repository versus data storage
Git is appropriate for code, configuration, documentation, and small nonrestricted fixtures. It is generally inappropriate for credentials, protected data, large source datasets, sensitive coordinates, caches, and nonredistributable files. Repository paths may point to approved external authoritative locations. Absolute personal paths must not be the only method of locating data.

title: Project and Data Structure
text:
Generated versus maintained objects
Identify whether each major object is manually maintained, received externally, generated deterministically, generated stochastically, cached, archived, or superseded. Generated artifacts should identify producing code and inputs.

title: Project and Data Structure
text:
Common failure modes

A “final” CSV is edited manually after the script ran.
Source and cleaned data are mixed in one directory.
Multiple unversioned files are named final.
A report depends on an undocumented object in a user workspace.
Temporary HPC output is treated as an authoritative result.
Staged data cannot be tied to a source snapshot.

title: Assumptions, Diagnostics, and Fit
text: Diagnostics are evidence about how a method behaves and where it may fail. They are not decorative figures and are not automatically pass/fail tests.

title: Assumptions, Diagnostics, and Fit
text:
Match checks to the method
Relevant checks may include residual patterns, distributional and variance assumptions, overdispersion, zero inflation, nonlinear relationships, influential observations, multicollinearity, independence or dependence, spatial or temporal autocorrelation, hierarchical structure, identifiability, unrealistic fitted values, instability under small changes, boundary estimates, and numerical warnings. Do not require every check for every analysis.

title: Assumptions, Diagnostics, and Fit
text:
Residuals
Residuals are differences between observed values and values represented or predicted by the model. Use graphical and numerical checks appropriate to the method. Look for systematic patterns, geographic clustering, temporal structure, changing variance, extreme observations, subgroup-specific failure, and unrepresented nonlinear behavior. Random-looking residuals do not prove that a scientific interpretation is correct.

title: Assumptions, Diagnostics, and Fit
Assumptions, Diagnostics, and Fit
text:
Fit is not prediction
A model may describe the data used to fit it well and still predict new data poorly. Separate in-sample fit, diagnostic adequacy, out-of-sample prediction, causal interpretation, and domain plausibility. A high R-squared value, low information criterion, small p-value, narrow credible interval, or visually appealing map is not sufficient validation.

title: Assumptions, Diagnostics, and Fit
text:
Model comparison
When several models were considered, record which were compared, why, what evidence was used, whether comparison occurred during Analyze or Validate, whether it changed the primary analysis, and which result version was retained. If validation evidence leads to a different model, return to Analyze and create a new analysis version.

title: Prediction and Forecast Validation
text: Use this guidance for predictive models, forecasts, risk maps, classifiers, early-warning systems, species or disease distribution predictions, spatial interpolation intended for prediction, and operational decision tools. Do not force predictive validation onto analyses that make no predictive claim.

title: Prediction and Forecast Validation
text: Use this guidance for predictive models, forecasts, risk maps, classifiers, early-warning systems, species or disease distribution predictions, spatial interpolation intended for prediction, and operational decision tools. Do not force predictive validation onto analyses that make no predictive claim.

title: Prediction and Forecast Validation
text:
Define the prediction task
Record prediction target, forecast horizon, geographic and temporal support, target population, prediction unit, update frequency, intended decision or user, and outcome prevalence or base rate where relevant.

title: Prediction and Forecast Validation
text:
Separate development and evaluation

Training data are used to estimate the model.
Tuning data are used to choose settings or model form.
Evaluation data are reserved for assessing performance.
External validation data come from a meaningfully different setting, population, location, or time.

Do not call evaluation external unless it is genuinely separate in a scientifically meaningful way.

title: Prediction and Forecast Validation
text:
Cross-validation and data leakage
Cross-validation repeatedly fits and evaluates a model using different data subsets. Random splitting may mislead when data are spatially clustered, temporally ordered, grouped by herd, facility, county, site, host, outbreak, or individual, repeatedly measured, or strongly autocorrelated. Use grouping, spatial blocking, temporal blocking, rolling-origin evaluation, or prospective evaluation when those better represent intended use.
Data leakage occurs when information from the evaluation period or units influences model development. Examples include calculating transformations using all years before splitting, using future observations in a forecast predictor, allowing the same individual or outbreak in both sets, selecting variables after viewing evaluation results, or using revised data unavailable at the historical forecast date.

title: Prediction and Forecast Validation
text:
Performance evidence
Choose measures that match the purpose. Evidence may include prediction error, absolute or squared error, calibration, discrimination, sensitivity and specificity, precision and recall, interval coverage, forecast sharpness, rank correlation, spatial accuracy, threshold utility, and decision consequences.
Calibration is agreement between predicted values or probabilities and observations. Discrimination is the ability to distinguish higher-risk from lower-risk observations. Interval coverage is how often observed outcomes fall inside stated uncertainty intervals. Do not prescribe one universal metric.

title: Prediction and Forecast Validation
text:
Baselines and scope
Compare with meaningful simple alternatives where possible: historical average, persistence, seasonal expectation, simple spatial or temporal model, current operational rule, or null model. A complex model should not be judged only against no model.
Distinguish retrospective reconstruction, hindcasting, rolling historical evaluation, prospective forecasting, and external evaluation. A retrospectively strong model is not automatically supported for prospective use.
Predictive support applies only to the evaluated population, geography, time period, forecast horizon, outcome definition, data availability conditions, and operational process.

title: Validation Decisions and Records
text: The validation plan records proposed questions, checks, evidence, and review. An individual check may be planned, completed, completed with limitation, failed, inconclusive, not applicable, or superseded. Planned means the check is identified but no finding is recorded. Completed means the check was performed and its finding is recorded. Check completion does not determine the overall conclusion by itself. The validation record, or an equivalent validation-level document, contains the authoritative overall conclusion. One major failed check may matter more than many minor successful checks.

title: Validation Decisions and Records
text: The validation plan records proposed questions, checks, evidence, and review. An individual check may be planned, completed, completed with limitation, failed, inconclusive, not applicable, or superseded. Planned means the check is identified but no finding is recorded. Completed means the check was performed and its finding is recorded. Check completion does not determine the overall conclusion by itself. The validation record, or an equivalent validation-level document, contains the authoritative overall conclusion. One major failed check may matter more than many minor successful checks.

title: Validation Decisions and Records
text:
Evidence synthesis
Summarize supporting evidence, conflicting evidence, failed checks, inconclusive checks, missing evidence, known limitations, reviewer concerns, relevance to intended use, and the consequence of remaining uncertainty.

title: Validation Decisions and Records
text:
Overall conclusion
Use only:

not yet evaluated — no conclusion has been recorded.
validation in progress — checks are underway.
supported for stated use — available evidence is sufficient for the identified use and scope.
supported for stated use with documented limitation — evidence supports a narrower or conditional use, and the limitation is visible to later users.
evidence inconclusive — evidence does not support a confident positive or negative conclusion.
not supported for stated use — material evidence contradicts the intended use, or essential evidence is absent and cannot be resolved.
superseded — a new analysis or validation record replaces this one.

title: Validation Decisions and Records
text:
Scope statement
Every substantive conclusion—supported for stated use, supported for stated use with documented limitation, evidence inconclusive, or not supported for stated use—must state the analysis ID and version, candidate result IDs, intended use, population or system, geographic scope, temporal scope, spatial or temporal resolution, forecast horizon where relevant, known limitations, and conditions requiring reevaluation. An inconclusive or not-supported conclusion is meaningful only in relation to the use and scope that were actually evaluated. A record that is not yet evaluated or validation in progress does not need a completed scope statement, but the intended scope should still be identified where known.

title: Validation Decisions and Records
text:
Returning to Analyze
When validation requires changes to data subsets, exclusions, model form, variables, priors, parameters, forecast target, spatial or temporal support, scenario definition, or output calculation, return to Analyze and create a new analysis version. Do not edit the validated candidate result in place.

title: Validation Decisions and Records
text:
Supersession and later stages
Supersession does not always imply a new analysis. A newer validation record may incorporate new external data, a later forecast period, an additional reviewer, or corrected validation evidence. Preserve the earlier record, mark it superseded, identify the replacement validation ID, and do not transfer the earlier conclusion automatically. Record a replacement analysis ID when the analysis also changed. A supported conclusion permits consideration in later Collaborate and Communicate stages; it does not provide publication, release, operational, policy, or data-sharing approval.

title: Verify Analysis and Outputs
text: Before judging whether a result is scientifically adequate, confirm that the intended analysis was actually carried out and that expected outputs are complete.

title: Verify Analysis and Outputs
Verify Analysis and Outputs
text:
Completeness
Check for missing runs, scenarios, chains, or replicates; incomplete time periods; missing spatial units; silently dropped records; failed job-array tasks; warnings; cancelled jobs; and manually replaced outputs. A successful command or zero exit code is not proof of completeness.

title: Verify Analysis and Outputs
Verify Analysis and Outputs
text:
Spatial and temporal checks
As applicable, confirm coordinate reference system, spatial extent, raster dimensions and alignment, geometry validity, temporal ordering, time-zone handling, epidemiological-week convention, forecast origin and horizon, no accidental overlap between training and evaluation periods, and no future information entering earlier predictions.

title: Verify Analysis and Outputs
text:
Simulation verification
For simulations and mechanistic models, use relevant checks such as benchmark cases, limiting cases, known equilibria, conservation or mass-balance checks, nonnegative constraints, expected response direction, parameter boundaries, simplified hand calculations, and deterministic behavior when randomness is disabled. These checks show whether the model was implemented as intended; they do not show that it adequately represents the real system.

title: Verify Analysis and Outputs
text:
Failed verification
When verification fails:

Record the failure.
Do not repair the candidate result silently.
Return to Analyze.
Create a new analysis version.
Rerun affected work and update candidate result records.
Repeat relevant validation checks.

This is an informational practice audit, not a quality score, ranking, or assessment of scientific correctness. It records observable repository and website practices and requires human review.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Review boundary
The audit reviewed the GeoEpi organization profile, the public organization website repository, the organization .github repository, the public Notebook repository, and eight purposively selected research repositories. The review date was 2026-08-05. The machine-readable observations are in standards/data/geoepi-repository-audit.csv.
The review examined public repository trees, READMEs, key workflow and documentation files, GitHub workflow directories, repository license metadata and license files, citation files or references, test paths, and plausible entry points. No code was executed and no scientific validation or compliance review was performed. A yes means that an artifact was visible and usable enough for this limited review; partial, unclear, and no do not imply that a practice is absent from private archives, external services, or project knowledge.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Organization references
The GeoEpi organization profile describes work on animal disease transmission and outbreak dynamics and links the group website and research notebook. The profile describes the Notebook as a living resource for reproducible science in scientific computing, coding, data management, and modeling, and explicitly says it is not a compendium of rigid requirements. The organization .github profile repeats this scope and points to OSF for project management, storage, version control, and archival support.
The organization website was reviewed for navigation, typography, neutral colors, logo/favicon assets, and the distinction between a research-group homepage and an operational notebook. Its research scope spans statistical and mathematical modeling, bioinformatics, artificial intelligence, and molecular-to-landscape scales. These observations inform limited visual continuity; they do not authorize copying the website structure or branding wholesale.

Workflow types represented
The sample covers spatial and spatiotemporal analysis, outbreak and surveillance analysis, ecological or field-adjacent data, genomics and phylogenetics, mathematical and simulation models, rendered supporting-information sites, interactive applications, and high-performance computing. That diversity supports a project standard based on traceability and handoff rather than a single folder tree or software stack.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Recurring documentation gaps
The sample showed inconsistent or hard-to-find records for software environments, data classification and restrictions, source-to-derived transformations, checksums or acquisition dates, output/run inventories, decision history, tests and CI, citation metadata, licenses, and closeout/handoff status. Several repositories contain useful rendered products but do not make the authoritative source, current execution path, or reproducibility boundary obvious from the top-level README.
These are aggregate observations from a limited public snapshot. A gap means that the item was not readily discoverable during this review; it does not mean that project members have not documented it elsewhere. This page is provisional, is based only on public repository contents, is not a compliance review, and is not a ranking.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Practices mature enough to standardize
The following are sufficiently cross-cutting to propose as minimum requirements: project identity and ownership; a current README; documented separation of source, staged, derived, code, configuration, documentation, outputs, logs, and temporary material; source-data protection; data provenance; data classification; data dictionaries; retained scripted transformations; version control with explicit exclusions; proportional environment records; explicit consequential parameters; quality checks appropriate to the workflow; result traceability; durable decision records; release readiness; and handoff/closeout records.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Recommended rather than universal
The following should remain recommended or conditional: one universal directory tree; renv for every R project; containers; continuous integration; unit-test coverage; workflow orchestration; formal metadata standards such as EML; checksums for every file; public release of data; notebooks as the primary execution format; OSF or any one storage provider; and a specific HPC scheduler. They become conditionally required when project sensitivity, scale, operational consequence, computational cost, publication commitments, or handoff risk makes them necessary.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Repository-specific patterns not generalized
Targets and Slurm manifest ledgers in EpiPlume, BEAST XML and cluster scripts in phylo-tutorial, Shiny delivery in seir-vector, and publication-oriented rendered sites in several repositories are valuable patterns but are not universal minimums. A repository may use Quarto, R Markdown, a workflow engine, a scheduler, a database, a notebook, or a scripted command-line entry point when the chosen path is documented and traceable.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Discrepancies and unresolved interpretation
Repositories differ in default branch name, whether rendered output is committed, where data are stored, whether a project is a tutorial or publication package, and whether an external archive is part of the authoritative workflow. Public repositories also expose only a subset of access-controlled data and institutional records. Human review is needed to decide institutional terminology for data classification, approved storage and retention, release review, licensing, authorship, and exception authority. These decisions are collected in Open policy decisions.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
External guidance used for comparison
The external comparison used the existing resource catalog, with access dates recorded there and here. The Turing Way emphasizes reproducible research, version control, data management, documentation, testing, review, and collaboration as connected practices. Good Enough Practices in Scientific Computing provides a deliberately pragmatic baseline for research computing. TIER Protocol 4.0 provides a replication-documentation model, while RDMkit organizes FAIR-oriented data management by lifecycle, role, domain, task, and tools.
The FAIR Principles and FAIR Principles for Research Software support findability, accessibility, interoperability, reuse, software quality, and citation. The CARE Principles add collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility, and ethics for Indigenous data. Government and domain-specific comparison points include USDA NAL data-management guidance, the CDC Field Epidemiology Manual, FGDC metadata guidance, GBIF georeferencing best practices, Ecological Metadata Language, and Ecological Forecasting Initiative standards.
These sources are guidance, standards, or community practices—not institutional policy. Where they conflict with USDA, laboratory, information-security, records-management, contractual, privacy, or data-governance requirements, the authoritative requirement controls and the project records the constraint.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Limitations
This is a point-in-time review of public repository material, not an audit of access-controlled archives, computational execution, scientific validity, or compliance. The CSV is intentionally descriptive and must not be used to score or rank repositories.

title: Open Policy Decisions
text:
Human approval required



This page records open decisions. It does not establish institutional policy or authorize a storage system, classification scheme, retention period, release process, or use of generative AI.
The owner, evidence, status, and review point below are role-based placeholders. No named individuals are assigned.

title: Open Policy Decisions
text:
Interim treatment
Record applicable restrictions without inventing official labels. Use the approved system named by the data owner or agreement. Do not upload restricted data, PII, credentials, unpublished confidential material, or protected research content to an unapproved service. Preserve upstream license terms and record uncertainty. Legal, privacy, security, contractual, and institutional requirements cannot be waived by a project exception.
Until approved, each item should receive an evidence-backed decision, decision date, and review date. The proposed standard should then be revised rather than silently converting assumptions into policy.
